NOTICE TO THE SHAREHOLDERS
Notice is hereby given that the 45th Annual General Meeting 
(AGM) of the Members of Apollo Hospitals Enterprise 
Limited will be held on Tuesday, the 25th day of August, 
2026 at 10.15 A.M. IST through Video Conferencing (“VC”) 
/ Other Audio-Visual Means (“OAVM”) to transact the 
following business:
ORDINARY BUSINESS:
ITEM NO. 1:
Adoption of Financial Statements for the financial year 
ended March 31, 2026.
To receive, consider and adopt:-
i. the audited standalone financial statements of the 
Company for the financial year ended March 31, 2026 
together with the reports of the Board of Directors and 
Auditors thereon;
ii. the audited consolidated financial statements of the 
Company for the financial year ended March 31, 2026 
together with the report of the Auditors thereon;
 and in this regard, to pass the following resolutions as 
Ordinary Resolutions:
(i) “RESOLVED THAT  the audited standalone financial 
statements of the Company for the financial year 
ended March 31, 2026, and the Report of the Board 
of Directors and Auditors’ thereon placed before this 
meeting, be and are hereby received, considered and 
adopted.”
(ii) “RESOLVED FURTHER THAT  the audited 
consolidated financial statements of the Company 
for the financial year ended March 31, 2026, and 
the Report of the Auditors thereon placed before this 
meeting, be and are hereby considered and adopted.”ITEM NO. 2:
Confirmation of Interim Dividend and approval for 
Declaration of Final Dividend.
To confirm payment of Interim Dividend and to declare 
final dividend on Equity Shares for the financial year ended 
March 31, 2026 and, in this regard, to pass the following 
resolutions as Ordinary Resolutions:
“RESOLVED THAT  the Interim Dividend of ` 10/- per equity 
share (200%) of face value of ` 5/- each for the financial 
year 2025-26, paid to the shareholders on February 27, 
2026 involving a gross amount of ` 1,437.85 million be and 
is hereby ratified.”
“RESOLVED FURTHER THAT  based on the 
recommendation of the Board of Directors of the Company 
a Final Dividend at the rate of ` 10/- per equity share (200%) 
of face value of ` 5/- each fully paid up, be and is hereby 
declared, out of the profits of the Company for the financial 
year ended March 31, 2026.”
ITEM NO. 3:
Re-appointment of Retiring Director.
To appoint a director in place of Smt. Sangita Reddy, 
(DIN:00006285) who retires by rotation and being eligible 
offers herself for re- appointment and in this regard, to pass 
the following resolution as an Ordinary Resolution:
“RESOLVED THAT  pursuant to Section 152 and other 
applicable provisions, if any, of the Companies Act, 2013, 
Smt. Sangita Reddy, (holding DIN: 00006285) who retires 
by rotation at this meeting and being eligible offers herself 
for re-appointment, be and is hereby re- appointed as a 
Director of the Company, liable to retire by rotation.”

4NOTES:
1. The Explanatory Statement pursuant to Section 102(1) 
of the Companies Act, 2013 (“the Act”) relating to 
special business to be transacted at the 45th Annual 
General Meeting (“AGM”), is annexed to the Notice.
2. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Government of 
India (“MCA”) vide its General Circular Nos. 20/2020, 
10/2022, 9/2023,  9/ 2024 and 03/2025 dated May 
05, 2020, December 28, 2022, September 25, 2023, 
September 19, 2024 and September 22, 2025, 
respectively, and other circulars issued in this respect 
(“MCA Circulars”) has allowed, inter-alia, conduct 
of AGMs through Video Conferencing/ Other Audio-
Visual Means (“VC/ OAVM”) facility, in accordance with 
the requirements provided in paragraphs 3 and 4 of 
the MCA General Circular No. 20/2020. In compliance 
with the provisions of Companies Act, 2013 (“the 
Act”), Securities and Exchange Board of India (“SEBI”) 
also vide its Circular No. SEBI/HO/CFD/CFD-PoD-
2/P/CIR/2024/133 dated October 03, 2024 (“SEBI 
Circular”) has provided relaxations from compliance 
with certain provisions of the SEBI (Listing Obligations 
and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 
(“Listing Regulations”). In compliance with these 
Circulars, applicable provisions of the Act and the 
Listing Regulations, the AGM of the Company is 
being held through VC/OAVM facility, which does not 
require physical presence of members at a common 
venue. The deemed venue for the AGM shall be the 
Registered Office of the Company.
3. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 105 of the Act, 
a Member entitled to attend and vote at the AGM is 
entitled to appoint a proxy to attend and vote on his/
her behalf and the proxy need not be a Member of the 
Company. Since this 45th AGM is being held pursuant 
to the MCA Circulars through VC / OAVM, physical 
attendance of Members has been dispensed with. 
Accordingly, the facility for appointment of proxies by 
the Members will not be available for the 45th AGM 
and hence the proxy form and attendance slip are not 
annexed to this Notice. However, the Body Corporates 
are entitled to appoint authorised representatives to 
attend the AGM through VC/OAVM and participate 
there at and cast their votes through e-voting.
4. The Members can join the 45th AGM in the VC / OAVM 
mode 15 minutes before and after the scheduled time 
of the commencement of the Meeting by following 
the procedure mentioned in the Notice. The facility of 
participation at the EGM/AGM through VC/OAVM will be made available for 1000 members on first come first 
served basis. This will not include large Shareholders 
(Shareholders holding 2% or more shareholding), 
Promoters, Institutional Investors, Directors, Key 
Managerial Personnel, the Chairpersons of the Audit 
Committee, Nomination and Remuneration Committee 
and Stakeholders Relationship Committee, Auditors 
etc. who are allowed to attend the AGM without 
restriction on account of first come first served basis.
5. Members attending the 45th AGM through VC / OAVM 
shall be counted for the purpose of reckoning the 
quorum under Section 103 of the Act.
6. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 108 of the 
Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 20 of the 
Companies (Management and Administration) 
Rules, 2014 (as amended)  the Secretarial Standard 
on General Meetings (SS-2) issued by the ICSI and 
Regulation 44 of SEBI (Listing Obligations & Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations 2015 (as amended), and 
the Circulars issued by the Ministry of Corporate 
Affairs from time to time the Company is providing 
facility of remote e-Voting to its Members in respect 
of the business to be transacted at the EGM/AGM. 
For this purpose, the Company has entered into an 
agreement with National Securities Depository Limited 
(NSDL) for facilitating voting through electronic means, 
as the authorised agency. The facility of casting votes 
by a member using remote e-Voting system as well as 
e-voting on the date of the EGM/AGM will be provided 
by NSDL.
7. In compliance with the aforesaid circulars issued 
by MCA and SEBI, notice of the 45th AGM along 
with the Annual Report 2025-2026 is being sent 
only through electronic mode to those Members 
whose email addresses are registered with the 
Company or Depository Participants. Additionally, 
in accordance with the Regulation 36(1)(b) of the 
SEBI (Listing Obligations & Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015, the Company is also sending a 
letter to shareholders whose e-mail addresses are not 
registered with the Company/Registrar/DP providing 
the weblink of Company’s website from where the 
Notice of the 45th AGM and Annual Report 2025-
2026 can be accessed. The Company shall send 
the physical copy of the Annual Report 2025-2026 
to those members who have made a request for the 
same. Any member who desires to get a physical 
copy of the Annual Report may request for the same 
by sending an email to the Company at investor.
relations@apollohospitals.com.

19. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 124 of the 
Companies Act, 2013, Investor Education and 
Protection Fund Authority (Accounting, Audit, Transfer 
and Refund) Rules, 2016 read with the relevant 
circulars and amendments thereto (“IEPF Rules”), the 
amount of dividend remaining unpaid or unclaimed 
for a period of seven years from the due date is required to be transferred to the Investor Education 
and Protection Fund (IEPF), constituted by the Central 
Government.
  Furthermore, the IEPF Rules mandate Companies 
to transfer shares of shareholders whose dividend 
amounts remain unpaid/ unclaimed for a period of 7 
consecutive years to the demat account of the IEPF 
Authority. The said requirement does not apply to 
shares in respect of which there is a specific order of 
the Court, Tribunal or Statutory Authority, restraining 
any transfer of shares.

The following Statement sets out all material facts relating to the Special Business mentioned in the accompanying Notice.
ITEM NO.5:
Dr. Prathap C. Reddy, the visionary founder of Apollo 
Hospitals, has served as the Company’s Chairman since 
its inception. Under his remarkable leadership, Apollo 
Hospitals has experienced phenomenal growth. Today, it 
is not only recognised as one of Asia’s leading healthcare 
service providers, but also stands tall as a constituent of the 
prestigious NIFTY 50 Index, signifying its position among 
India’s largest companies. This impressive trajectory is a 
testament to Dr. Reddy’s dedication and strategic direction. 
Further solidifying his leadership, a recent recognition by 
Business World magazine placed Apollo Hospitals among 
the top 5 most respected companies within the top 20 of 
India.
Given this exceptional track record and ongoing commitment 
to excellence, the Board of Directors strongly endorse the 
re-appointment of Dr. Prathap C. Reddy as Chairman for a 
further period of two years up to June 24, 2028.
Apollo Hospitals’ journey
The Group, with its network of over 10,900 beds across 
78 hospitals in culturally diverse locations in India, employs 
over 10,000 top class clinicians. It is one of the largest 
hospital groups in the world, consistently ranked among the 
best for advanced medical services. These hospitals have 
served over 200 million patients from 150 countries, with 
eight receiving the prestigious JCI accreditation. 
Dr. Prathap C. Reddy’s vision extended beyond hospitals, 
aiming to create an integrated ecosystem of care. Under 
his dynamic leadership, the Apollo Hospitals Group 
has established over 7,200 pharmacies, 2,500 retail 
touchpoints, and over 47 million registered users on the 
digital platform Apollo 24/7. 
The Apollo Group, initially identified as a healthcare provider, 
is now a leading provider of comprehensive healthcare 
solutions, including next-generation healthcare IT services. 
These efforts have helped establish a modern healthcare 
network through both in-house and outreach services, 
reaching millions of people. 
Shareholders wealth has increased at a compounded 
average annual growth rate (“CAGR”) of 40% over the last 
5 years as compared to 16% CAGR for the Nifty 50 index. ROCE on a consolidated basis (without reckoning for Capital 
WIP) increased from 20% in FY 24 to 23.7% in FY 26 Return 
on Equity on a consolidated basis (without reckoning for 
AHL where the digital healthcare platform business is still 
in the start up phase ) increased from 15.7% in FY 24 to 
19.6% in FY 26. Consolidated EBITDA increased by 25% in 
FY 26 as compared to FY 25
Rationale for Re-appointment
The Board has decided to re-appoint Dr. Prathap C. 
Reddy to support the responsible and prudent oversight 
of the proposed demerger and separate listing of Apollo 
Healthtech Limited, a significant strategic transformation 
intended to sharpen the focus of the respective businesses 
and support long-term value creation. As the founder of 
Apollo Hospitals, Dr. Reddy has shaped the Group’s long-
term vision, healthcare delivery model and institutional 
standing. His deep knowledge of the Group and the 
strategic direction underpinning its evolution is particularly 
valuable as the transaction moves from approval into 
implementation and the two businesses prepare to operate 
with greater strategic focus.
Dr. Prathap C. Reddy has also developed longstanding 
relationships and credibility across the wider healthcare 
and public-policy ecosystem, including with public 
institutions, medical bodies, industry participants and 
strategic partners. Following the recommendation of the 
NRC, which comprises solely Independent Directors, 
the Board unanimously concluded that his continued 
leadership, sector standing and institutional network would 
support effective stakeholder engagement, preserve the 
vision underpinning the transaction and help ensure that 
the demerger and separate listing are implemented in an 
orderly and prudent manner.
This continuity complements, rather than displaces, 
the Company’s established succession framework. The 
Company maintains clearly defined roles and responsibilities 
across its executive leadership, together with planned and 
contingency succession arrangements for the Executive 
Directors. Accordingly, Dr. Prathap C. Reddy’s re-
appointment reflects a considered approach to leadership 
continuity during this period of strategic change, supported 
by the Company’s established succession arrangements.

15Dr. Prathap C. Reddy has devoted his full time to the 
Company since its inception. Since 1997, the members 
have approved his remuneration for five-year terms, with 
the most recent approval granted at the Annual General 
Meeting on August 30, 2024, with close to 95% shareholder 
support. This approval covered a period of two years, 
ending on June 24, 2026.
According to the Companies Act, 2013, a whole-time 
director can be appointed for a tenure not exceeding five 
years at a time. Therefore, it is proposed to re-appoint  
Dr. Prathap C. Reddy as a Whole-time director designated 
as Executive Chairman for a period not exceeding two years. 
In re-appointing Dr. Prathap C. Reddy as the Executive 
Chairman, the NRC consisting entirely of Independent 
Directors has carefully considered his expertise, background, 
experience, and substantial contributions during his tenure 
with the Company.
During the year, under his strategic leadership, the Company 
delivered strong financial and operational performance, 
with:
-  Consolidated Revenue up 16%, to ` 252,285 million 
for the year. 
-  EBITDA up 25%, to ` 37,693 million for the year.
-  A robust credit profile (long-term ratings ICRA 
AAA, CRISIL AA+ and India Rating AA+), reiterating 
the Company’s prudent capital allocation policy and 
sound balance sheet management position.
-  Quality and Clinical Excellence standards achieved 
during the year being comparable to global healthcare 
excellence benchmarks. More details are available in 
the Clinical Governance section.
-  Net Promoter Score / Patient Satisfaction, recorded 
during the year was 74 as compared to target of 71 
resulting in a 104% achievement.
-  ESG measures, more specifically efforts relating to 
Energy Efficiency and Gender Parity Measures, were 
met. During the period under review, the Company 
achieved a 10% reduction in energy intensity metrics 
across KPIs under Scope 1 and Scope 2 emission 
parameters. With regard to Gender Parity, the 
Company achieved a gender parity score of 56% 
which was as per the targeted plan.Dr. Prathap C. Reddy’s Profile
Dr. Prathap C. Reddy holds a Bachelor’s degree in Medicine 
and Surgery from Stanley Medical College, Madras, 
India, and is a Fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons, 
Edinburgh, United Kingdom. He practiced as a cardiologist 
in the USA before founding Apollo Hospitals, embarking on 
an extraordinary journey that revolutionised healthcare and 
pioneered the private healthcare industry in India. Over the 
past 50 years, Dr. Reddy’s work in Indian healthcare has 
been driven by a strong sense of purpose-ensuring health 
and happiness for all.
Dr. Reddy is also passionate about a holistic approach to 
community development. The Total Health Foundation, an 
innovative population health model in Aragonda, Andhra 
Pradesh, aims to uplift individuals physically, mentally, 
emotionally, financially, and spiritually, building inclusive 
communities. The program’s impressive results have been 
documented by prestigious institutions like the Harvard 
School of Public Health.
Awards and Recognitions
Dr. Prathap C. Reddy has received numerous accolades in 
recognition of his outstanding contributions to healthcare. 
The Government of India bestowed upon him the Padma 
Bhushan in 1991 and the Padma Vibhushan, the country’s 
second highest civilian award, in 2010, for his transformative 
impact on the Indian healthcare industry.
Beyond these national honors, Dr. Reddy has been 
recognised globally. He was named Citizen of the Year by 
Mother Teresa in 1993-94 and received the Sir Nilrattan 
Sircar Memorial Oration Award for medical excellence in 
1998 by the Journal of the Indian Medical Association. 
Business India magazine also included him in their list of 
fifty most influential personalities who shaped India in its first 
fifty years since independence.
In 2022, Dr. Reddy was conferred the Lifetime Achievement 
Award by Forbes India, The Economic Times, and Business 
Standard for his pioneering work in transforming India’s 
healthcare landscape. The Government of India further 
acknowledged Apollo Hospitals Group’s monumental 
contributions by issuing a commemorative stamp, a rare 
honour for a healthcare organisation.

Smt. Rama Bijapurkar is currently a Professor of

economy, consumption and citizen environment for use in

is also an experienced independent director and has served 
on the boards of several of India's bluechip companies

governing councils of academic institutions, and regulatory 
bodies.

In order to augment long term resources for financing, inter 
alia ongoing capital expenditure, expansion activities of the 
Company and for general corporate purposes, the Board 
may at an appropriate time, offer or invite subscription 
for secured/unsecured redeemable non-convertible 
debentures in one or more series/ tranches on a private 
placement basis for a sum aggregating upto ` 7,500 million 
(Rupees Seven Thousand and Five Hundred million Only). 
This would be within the overall approved borrowing limit 
of ` 38,500 million (Rupees Thirty-Eight Thousand Five 
Hundred million Only).
Rule 14 of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of 
Securities) Rules, 2014 prescribed inter alia under Section 
42 of the Companies Act, 2013 (“the Act”) deals with 
private placement of securities by a Company. Sub-rule 
(1) of the said Rule 14 states that in case of an offer or 
invitation to subscribe for non-convertible debentures on a 
private placement basis, the Company shall obtain the prior 
approval of its shareholders by means of a special resolution 
only once in a year for all the offers or invitations for such 
issuance of non-convertible debentures during the year. 
Rule 18 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) 
Rules, 2014 deals with issue of secured debentures.
The Board will decide appropriately whether to issue 
debentures on a secured or unsecured basis.
Accordingly, consent of the members is being sought for 
passing a Special Resolution as set out at Item No. 7 of 
the Notice. This would enable the Board of the Company 
to offer or invite subscription for unsecured/ secured non-convertible debentures, as may be required by the 
Company, from time to time, for a period of one year from 
the date of passing this resolution.
The Board recommends the resolution as set out in Item 
No.7 of the accompanying Notice for approval of the 
Members by way of Special Resolution.
None of the Directors and Key Managerial Personnel of the 
Company and their relatives are in any way concerned or 
interested, financially or otherwise in the special resolution 
set out under Item No.7 of the Notice.

Chairman.Management Message
Dear Members,
Healthcare is entering one of the 
most transformative periods in its 
history
. For generations, medicine 
has advanced by responding to 
illness after it appeared. Today, we 
have the opportunity to reshape 
that journey by anticipating risk 
earlier and preserving health 
for longer.
This transformation is occurring 
through the thoughtful 
convergence of clinical excellence, 
scientiﬁc discovery and digital 
innovation. One truth remains 
unchanged: technology may 
enhance our capabilities, but 
compassion, judgement and 
human connection will always 
remain the foundation of healing. 
Despite making remarkable 
progress in improving life 
expectancy and expanding access 
to quality healthcare, the rising 
incidence of non-communicable 
diseases remains a core concern. 
Cardiovascular disease, diabetes 
and cancer now account for nearly 
63% of all deaths in India, with cardiovascular diseases emerging 
as the leading cause, responsible for 
almost 28% of total mortality. This 
calls for a fundamental shift from 
episodic treatment to continuous 
health management, early detection 
and personalised care. 
At Apollo, we are advancing this 
vision by bringing together clinical 
leadership with the powerful triad of 
Intelligence, Intent and Impact. 
Guided by these principles, we 
are committed to creating a more 
personalised path to better health for 
every individual who places their trust 
in our hands.
The Foundation of Care
Intent is the purpose that gives the 
practice of medicine its direction. 
It is the conscious commitment to 
look beyond the immediate condition, 
understand what matters to each 
patient, and make every decision with 
a clear purpose: to deliver care that is 
precise, personalised, compassionate 
and centred on the individual.An Intelligent Healthcare 
Ecosystem 
Intent delivers its greatest value 
when combined with intelligence. 
At Apollo, we are building an 
intelligent healthcare ecosystem by 
combining technology with clinical 
expertise, enabling our caregivers 
to deliver evidence-based care with 
greater consistency and precision. 
This integrated approach helps give 
every patient the same high standards 
of care, wherever they live or however 
they access our services.
Over the past year, we have 
further strengthened our AI-led 
capabilities. Our proprietary Clinical 
Intelligence Engine has evolved into 
a valuable clinical decision support 
platform, while our cloud-enabled 
digital infrastructure, AI-powered 
radiology, intelligent diagnostic 
workﬂows and real-time clinical 
dashboards are enhancing clinical 
precision, operational efﬁciency and 
patient safety.

Predict. Prevent. Protect.Operating Context
The future of healthcare lies not only in treating disease, but 
also in preventing it before it begins. As non-communicable 
diseases (NCDs) continue to emerge earlier and become more 
prevalent across India, the imperative to shift from reactive 
treatment to proactive prevention has never been greater.
This focus underpins the Health of the Nation Initiative, an evidence-based 
r
eport that draws on insights from Apollo Hospitals’ extensive preventive healthcare 
ecosystem to understand evolving disease patterns, promote early detection and 
enable timely intervention. Now in its sixth edition, analysing more than three million 
preventive health assessments, the report reveals a rapidly evolving healthcare 
landscape shaped by lifestyle-related risks, earlier disease onset and changing 
patient expectations. Its ﬁndings reinforce the need for predictive, personalised 
and technology-enabled healthcare that identiﬁes risks sooner, enables timely 
intervention and advances the journey from illness to wellness.

Daily Tiered Huddles
Evolution Timeline
In less than two years, we have rapidly transformed our Daily Tiered 
Huddles from a structured safety review programme into an AI-enabled 
clinical governance platform. Through continuous reﬁnement, 
rapid scale-up and workﬂow automation, we have empowered our 
clinicians with real-time insights, faster decision-making and stronger 
accountability across our hospital network.
Daily Tiered Huddles form the 
backbone of our real-time clinical 
and operational governance, 
bringing multi-disciplinary teams 
together daily to review patient care, 
safety indicators and operational 
priorities. This structured approach 
enables timely escalation of critical 
issues, strengthens cross-functional 
coordination and supports consistent, 
high-quality care across our network.
This strengthens Root Cause 
Analysis, accelerates corrective and 
preventive actions, and ensures timely 
follow-up through automated tracking 
of compliance and action ownership. 
For our patients, it enables earlier 
risk identiﬁcation, quicker clinical interventions and greater adherence 
to safety protocols, contributing to 
safer and more consistent care. Every 
non-compliance item is assigned to 
an accountable owner, with progress 
tracked through structured follow-up. 
Cross-hospital advisories are veriﬁed 
through virtual audits, while units receive monthly performance 
scores. Critical safety events are 
escalated to senior leadership 
within 24 hours, reinforcing 
accountability and continuous 
quality improvement.
Earlier Detection Safer Patients
Better Outcomes Faster Action
Daily Tiered Huddles create a proactive system for identifying and addressing patient care risks before they 
escalate. By bringing frontline caregivers and leaders together every day, potential concerns are recognised 
earlier, decisions are made faster, and actions are tracked to closure.
For clinicians, this means greater visibility of patient risks, improved multi-disciplinary collaboration, faster 
escalation of critical issues and a stronger culture of accountability and safety. For patients, it translates into 
safer care, earlier intervention, fewer preventable complications, better coordinated treatment and quicker 
resolution of concerns.
The cumulative impact is a high-reliability healthcare environment where risks are managed proactively 
rather than retrospectively, driving better patient outcomes, reducing clinical risk and strengthening 
organisational governance.

Clinical Mastery at Work.Success Stories
Every patient journey is unique. These landmark clinical achievements 
demonstrate how innovation, expertise and compassionate car
e are 
transforming outcomes.
Saving a High-Risk Heart through Keyhole Precision
A 53-year-old woman suffering from severe damage to both her aortic and mitral valves due to 
infective endocarditis was considered a very high-risk candidate for conventional open-heart 
surgery because of multiple underlying health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis, obesity, a 
thyroid disorder and a previous stroke.
To minimise surgical risk while ensuring the best possible outcome, the clinical team performed 
India's ﬁrst robotic double valve replacement using a completely endoscopic approach. 
Through a few small keyhole incisions between the ribs, the damaged valves were replaced with 
bio-prosthetic valves using advanced robotic technology and real-time imaging guidance, avoiding 
the need to open the chest. The procedure was completed with exceptional precision, minimal 
blood loss and no complications.
The patient's recovery was remarkably quick. She was breathing on her own and walking within 
12 hours of surgery, shifted to the ward shortly thereafter, and discharged just three days later. 
At her one-week follow-up, she had recovered well and was free from symptoms, highlighting 
the potential of robotic cardiac surgery to transform outcomes for even the most complex, high-
risk patients.
A Made-in-India CAR-T Therapy Turns the Tide on Relapsed Leukaemia 
A 31-year-old engineer was diagnosed with high-risk Pre-B Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) 
in September 2024. Despite undergoing several cycles of intensive chemotherapy, small amounts 
of leukemia cells remained in his body, indicating that the disease had not responded completely 
to treatment.
Considering the aggressive nature of his condition, he was considered suitable for CAR-T cell 
therapy. After receiving preparatory chemotherapy with ﬂudarabine and cyclophosphamide, he 
underwent an India-developed and India-manufactured CAR-T cell therapy, helping make this 
advanced treatment more affordable and accessible for patients with difﬁcult-to-treat blood cancers. 
This marked the hospital's ﬁrst CAR-T cell therapy for Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia, representing 
an important milestone in the treatment of adult leukemia. Following the infusion, he experienced 
only a mild immune reaction, which was successfully managed with standard supportive care. 
He did not develop any neurological complications or other serious side effects. Since the treatment, 
he has remained clinically stable, with early signs indicating good disease control.
Annual Report 2025-26 38
Deep Brain Stimulation Gives a 4-Year-Old Relief from Relentless 
Spasms 
A young child born with dystonic cerebral palsy experienced severe involuntary neck muscle 
contractions that caused constant pain, stiffness and spasms, making it difﬁcult for him to sit, 
eat or sleep comfortably. After medications failed to provide relief, his family was left with very 
few treatment options. The clinical team performed Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS), a highly 
specialised procedure that is rarely undertaken in children under the age of six. This made him one 
of the youngest patients in the world, and the ﬁrst in India, to undergo DBS for dystonia. Using 
advanced precision-guided technology, surgeons implanted tiny electrodes in the area of the brain 
responsible for controlling movement. These electrodes were connected to a Boston Scientiﬁc 
Vercise Genus P16 neurostimulator, which helps regulate abnormal brain signals and improve 
movement control.
While the procedure did not cure his underlying cerebral palsy, it signiﬁcantly reduced 
the painful spasms and muscle rigidity, allowing him to sit, rest and sleep more comfortably. 
The case represents a signiﬁcant milestone in Indian paediatric functional neurosurgery and 
a rare achievement globally for a child of his age.A Fertility-Sparing Answer to Cervical Cancer against the Odds 
A 38-year-old patient from Ghana, with one prior child by caesarean section and a BMI of 
66.7 kg/m², presented with cancer of the cervix. Robotic Fertility-Preserving Surgery was 
performed with Sentinel Node Mapping and colposcopy-guided conization of the cervix, achieving 
negative margins despite the added surgical difﬁculty posed by her morbid obesity. This was the 
ﬁrst case of robotic fertility-preserving surgery for cervical cancer with morbid obesity performed 
at Apollo. The patient was rendered cancer-free without requiring adjuvant radiation and she was 
well enough to travel back to Ghana within a week of surgery.
Turning a Rare Cardiac Emergency into a Life Saved 
A 23-year-old man was admitted after experiencing sudden breathlessness, along with mild fever 
and body aches, while trekking at an altitude of around 8,000 feet. Initial evaluation suggested 
a serious heart condition due to low oxygen levels, a rapid heartbeat and signs of strain on the 
heart. Further tests revealed that the right side of his heart was under signiﬁcant stress. Advanced 
imaging conﬁrmed a large blood clot blocking the main artery supplying blood to the lungs 
(known as a saddle pulmonary embolism), a rare and life-threatening medical emergency requiring 
immediate intervention. The case is recognised as the ﬁrst of its kind to be reported in Karnataka, 
highlighting the importance of rapid diagnosis and timely intervention in managing rare and critical 
cardiovascular emergencies.

Our Tender Loving Care Stories
A young child was brought to Apollo BGS Hospital, 
Mysore, with severe respiratory distress after days 
of persistent illness. On arrival, the emergency team 
responded immediately, initiating oxygen support and 
treatment to stabilise the child’s condition. Within 
48 hours, the child’s health improved signiﬁcantly, 
bringing relief to the family.
During a routine interaction, the care team learned 
about the family’s difﬁcult circumstances and the child’s 
heartfelt dream of owning a bicycle. Moved by the 
story, hospital teams came together to make that wish 
a reality. Working with local partners, they arranged a 
brand-new bicycle and surprised the child on the day 
of discharge.
The joy on the child’s face transformed the hospital 
corridor into a celebration. What began as a medical 
journey ended with a moment of hope, one that 
brought smiles not only to the child and family, but also 
to every caregiver who had been part of the recovery.At Apollo Hospitals, every member of our team plays 
a vital role in safeguarding lives, both inside and 
beyond our hospital walls. When a ﬁre broke out at a 
neighbouring commercial establishment close to Apollo 
Hospitals, Indore, our security team responded without 
hesitation. Even before emergency services arrived, 
they swiftly activated safety protocols, assisted with 
evacuation, managed the growing crowd and worked 
to contain the situation using available ﬁre safety 
equipment. Their calm, coordinated response helped 
prevent the ﬁre from escalating and protected patients, 
visitors, staff and surrounding communities from 
potential harm.
The incident demonstrated that healthcare extends 
beyond clinical excellence. It is equally deﬁned by 
vigilance, preparedness and the willingness to act when 
every second counts.
For a three-year-old undergoing treatment for Acute 
Myeloid Leukemia (AML), hospital visits became a little 
brighter because of something simple: his love for caps. 
The care team noticed how much joy they brought 
him, and what began as a small detail soon became 
a meaningful way to bring moments of happiness and 
familiarity into an otherwise difﬁcult treatment journey. 
 
One day, a member of the housekeeping team 
decided to make that joy more personal, crafting a cap 
especially for the child. It was a gesture beyond routine 
responsibility, but one that meant deeply to him and his 
family. When he received the handmade cap, his delight 
was immediate, a reminder that healing is not only 
about medical treatment, but also about the kindness, 
empathy and human connection that can make a 
difﬁcult journey feel a little lighter.One evening, a healthcare professional was 
approached by a neighbour whose father had suddenly 
experienced severe discomfort. After reviewing his ECG 
report, she immediately recognised the urgency of the 
situation. Without losing time, she coordinated with 
the emergency team, facilitated the admission process 
and alerted the concerned clinician, ensuring that 
everything was in place even before the patient reached 
the hospital. 
 
Further evaluation conﬁrmed a mild heart attack, 
and timely medical intervention and surgery helped 
the patient recover without delay. What could have 
become a critical situation was managed effectively 
through prompt judgement, coordinated action and a 
strong sense of responsibility. The incident reﬂects a 
culture where care extends beyond the workplace and 
where being there at the right moment can make all 
the difference.

Centre for Digital 
Health and Precision 
Medicine (CDHPM)
Established as a collaboration 
between Apollo University
, AHEL 
and University of Leicester (UK), 
CDHPM is emerging as a key 
hub for AI-enabled healthcare 
innovation. From Biobank to Breakthrough 
Sapien, Apollo Hospitals’ advanced biobank and precision medicine research 
platform, is recognised among the world’s top 10 biobanks. Housing over 
300,000 clinically annotated patient samples, it provides a powerful foundation 
for precision medicine, biomarker discovery and translational research, 
accelerating the development of more personalised and data-driven healthcare. 
By integrating high-quality biospecimens with clinical data under robust ethical 
and governance frameworks, Sapien is accelerating the development of 
personalised diagnostics, targeted therapies, and next-generation drug discovery.
Our expanding digital pathology platform further strengthens this ecosystem, 
with more than 3,000 cancer and 200 other disease pathology slides digitised 
into a high-resolution repository. Combined with advanced AI-driven analytics, 
these capabilities serve as powerful tools for clinicians, helping translate complex 
research insights into actionable clinical outcomes. By enabling biomarker 
discovery, predictive model validation and companion diagnostics, they help 
bridge the journey from scientiﬁc discovery to more informed, precise and 
meaningful patient care.
Transforming Patient Samples into Therapeutic Insights
To accelerate translational oncology research, Sapien expanded its portfolio 
of proprietary patient-derived cell (PDC) models for ovarian and lung cancers. 
The ovarian cancer programme comprises approximately 12 molecularly 
characterised PDC models, developed using whole-exome sequencing (WES) to 
correlate genomic alterations with drug response. During the year, lung cancer 
PDC models were also established using well-annotated patient samples, 
enabling physiologically relevant drug sensitivity assessment and pilot screening. 
Together, these integrated genomics and functional screening capabilities are 
strengthening the evaluation of novel therapeutics and advancing precision 
oncology research.

Energy Management
Reliable and affordable energy is fundamental to the quality 
of care we deliver. During FY 2025-26, we increased our 
renewable energy consumption by 18% to 236,416 GJ, 
taking renewables to around 30% of our total energy 
mix, while improving our energy intensity by ~12% to 
0.0000038 GJ per ` of turnover. Through renewable 
energy procurement, operational efﬁciency and digital 
optimisation, we continue to strengthen clinical resilience, 
lower our environmental footprint and improve long-term 
cost efﬁciency. 
Renewable Energy Procurement
We continue to accelerate our transition towards 
cleaner energy by expanding renewable electricity 
procurement across our hospitals. During FY 2025-26, 
we sourced 177,375.32 GJ of wind energy through 
long-term Power Purchase Agreements and consumed 
59,040.90 GJ of solar energy, taking our total renewable 
energy consumption to 236,416 GJ, an 18% increase 
over the previous year. This transition strengthens our 
decarbonisation journey while improving energy security 
and cost resilience.

Water Stewardship
We continue to strengthen water stewardship by improving 
recycling, treatment and circular water use across our 
operations. During FY 2025-26, 32.15% of our water 
demand was met through recycled water, supported 
by advanced treatment technologies and Zero Liquid 
Dishcharge (ZLD) systems at six facilities. These initiatives 
are helping us reduce freshwater dependence while 
building long-term operational resilience. 
Waste Management
We remain committed to responsible waste management 
through effective segregation, treatment and circularity 
initiatives. During FY 2025-26, we reduced our total waste 
generation by 3.1% to 14,553.50 MT, while improving 
waste intensity by ~15%. We also continued to ensure 
that 100% of our biomedical waste was segregated at 
source and treated through authorised CPCB-approved 
facilities, reinforcing our commitment to safe and compliant 
healthcare operations.

Snapshot of The Apollo Foundation
Established in 2013, Apollo Foundation serves as the philanthropic arm of Apollo Hospitals, driving inclusive and 
sustainable community development thr
ough its Total Health model. Operating across rural and tribal regions of Andhra 
Pradesh, Telangana, Tripura, Meghalaya, Assam and Arunachal Pradesh, the Foundation adopts an integrated approach 
that addresses preventive and curative healthcare alongside nutrition, mental well-being, water and sanitation, livelihood 
enhancement and education. 
During FY 2025–26, the Foundation's efforts were recognised by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government 
of India, which conferred upon it the status of Ni-kshay Mitra under the Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyan for its 
contribution towards the national mission of a TB-free India.

MATERIAL CHANGES AND COMMITMENTS 
AFFECTING THE COMP
ANY
Composite Scheme of Arrangement
The Board of Directors, at its meeting held on June 30, 
2025, approved the Composite Scheme of Arrangement 
amongst Apollo Hospitals Enterprise Limited (“Company”), 
Apollo Healthco Limited (“Transferor Company 1”), Keimed 
Private Limited (“Transferor Company 2”), and Apollo 
Healthtech Limited (“Resultant Company”) (the “Scheme”).
The Company received the approval of the Competition 
Commission of India on September 23, 2025, for approving 
the combination proposed under the Scheme. The 
Company has also received observation letters containing 
“No Objection” from BSE Limited and National Stock 
Exchange of India Limited, dated December 24, 2025 and 
December 23, 2025, respectively.
Subsequently, the Company, Transferor Company 1, 
Transferor Company 2, and the Resultant Company jointly 
/f_iled Application No. CA (CAA) / 8 / (CHE) / 2026 under 
Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013 before the 
Hon’ble National Company Law Tribunal, Chennai Bench, 
seeking directions to convene meetings of the equity 
shareholders and creditors in connection with the proposed 
Scheme.

Proposal to create one of India’s largest integrated 
Maternity and Fertility Care Platforms
The Board of Directors, at the meeting held on May 
20,2026 approved the proposal for Apollo Health and 
Lifestyle Limited (“AHLL”), a wholly owned subsidiary of the 
Company, to combine with Kids Clinic India Limited, which 
operates under the brand name “Cloudnine”, to create one 
of India’s largest maternity and fertility care platforms in 
India. As part of this arrangement, AHLL will divest its stake 
in its subsidiaries, namely Apollo Specialty Hospitals Private 
Limited and Apollo Fertility Centre Private Limited, to Kids 
Clinic India Limited at an enterprise value of approximately 
` 15,500 million, comprising cash of ` 7,650 million and 
an equity stake of around 9.9% in Kids Clinic India Limited 
valued at ` 7,850 million. The transaction is subject to 
receipt of approval from the Competition Commission of 
India.
Merger of Apollo Hospitals North Limited into the 
Company
The Board of Directors, at its meeting held on May 20, 2026, 
approved the proposal for the merger of Apollo Hospitals 
North Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of the Company, 
with and into Apollo Hospitals Enterprise Limited (“Holding 
Company” or the “Company”) under Section 230-232 of 
the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rules thereunder.
The proposed merger is subject to receipt of the necessary 
statutory and regulatory approvals, including the approval 
of the Hon’ble National Company Law Tribunal, Chennai 
Bench in accordance with the provisions of the Companies 
Act, 2013.

and will aggregate to a sum of ` 2,875.70 million (400%

2025, dividends paid by the Company shall be taxable

Corporate Governance Report
[Pursuant to Part C of Schedule V to the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and 
Disclosur
e Requirements) Regulations, 2015]
1.  THE COMPANY’S PHILOSOPHY ON CODE OF 
GOVERNANCE
 The basic objective of the corporate governance 
policies adopted by the Company is to attain the 
highest levels of transpar
ency, accountability and 
integrity. This objective extends not merely to comply 
with statutory requirements but also to go beyond 
them by putting into place procedures and systems, 
which are in accordance with the best practices of 
governance. Apollo believes that good corporate 
governance enhances the trust and con/f_idence of 
all the stakeholders. Good practice in corporate 
behaviour helps to enhance and maintain public trust 
in companies and the stock markets.
 Apollo reviews its corporate governance practices 
and disclosures to ensure that they re/f_lect the latest 
developments in the corporate arena, positioning 
itself to conform to the international best corporate 
governance practices. Apollo is committed to pursuing 
excellence in all its activities and in maximisation of 
shareholders’ wealth.
 The Company’s corporate governance policies and 
practices focus on the following principles:
1. To recognise the respective roles and 
responsibilities of the Board and management. 
2. To achieve the highest degree of transparency by 
maintaining a high degree of disclosure levels. 
3. To ensure and maintain high ethical standards in 
its functioning. 
4. To accord the highest importance to stakeholders’ 
relations, including investors. 
5. To ensure a sound system of risk management 
and internal controls. 
6. To ensure that employees of the Company 
subscribe to the corporate values and apply 
them in their conduct. 
7. To ensure that the decision-making process is 
fair and transparent. 
8. To ensure that the Company follows globally 
recognised corporate governance best practices. Governance Structure
 Apollo’s governance structure broadly comprises of the 
Board of Directors (the “Board”) and the Committees 
of the Board at the apex level and the management 
structure at the operational level. This layered structure 
brings about a harmonious blend in governance as the 
Board sets the overall corporate objectives and gives 
direction and freedom to the Management to achieve 
these corporate objectives within a given framework, 
thereby bringing about an enabling environment 
for value creation through sustainable pro/f_itable 
growth through a strong and independent oversight 
mechanism. 
 The Board plays a pivotal role in ensuring that the 
Company runs on sound and ethical business 
practices and that its resources are utilized for 
creating sustainable growth and societal wealth. The 
Board operates within the framework of a well-de/f_ined 
responsibility matrix which enables it to discharge 
its /f_iduciary duties of safeguarding the interests of 
the Company, ensuring fairness in the decision-
making process and integrity and transparency in the 
Company’s dealing with its stakeholders, including 
shareholders. 
 With a view to have a more focused attention on 
various facets of business and for better accountability, 
the Board has constituted the following committees 
viz. Audit Committee, Stakeholders’ Relationship 
Committee, Nomination and Remuneration 
Committee, Risk Management Committee, Corporate 
Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, 
Investment Committee, Innovation and Quality 
Committee. Each of these Committees have been 
mandated to operate within a given framework. 
 A Management structure for running the business of 
the Company as a whole is in place with appropriate 
delegation of powers and responsibilities.
2. BOARD OF DIRECTORS
 The Company has an Executive Chairman and a 
separate Managing Dir
ector, thereby ensuring the 
two key leadership roles are separated and not

Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (Listing Regulations), 
in case of an Executive Chairman, independent 
directors should comprise at least half of the Board 
Independent Directors, including independent woman

The Company’s Board has met both the independence

 The Board maintains a healthy blend of executive and 
non-executive directors, balancing strategic expertise 
with independent oversight and decision-making, 
which is continuously reviewed to ensure that there is a 
healthy level of refreshment. There is no predetermined 
allocation of Board seats, nor any /f_ixed split between

recommendations of the fully independent Nomination

d)  Policy for selection of Directors and their 
remuneration 
  The NRC has adopted a Charter which, inter alia, deals 
with the manner of selection of Non-Executive Directors 
and Executive Directors and their remuneration. This 
Policy is accordingly derived from the said Charter. 
 1.  Criteria for selection of Non-Executive 
Directors and Independent Directors;
a. Non-Executive Independent Directors 
shall be persons of high integrity with 
relevant expertise and experience so as 
to have a diverse Board with Directors 
having expertise in the /f_ields of healthcare, 
technology, marketing, /f_inance, taxation, 
law, governance and general management.
b. In case of appointment of Non-Executive 
Independent Directors, the NRC shall satisfy 
itself with regard to the independent nature 
of the Directors vis-à-vis the Company so 
as to enable the Board to discharge its 
functions and duties effectively.
c. The NRC shall ensure that the candidate 
identi/f_ied for appointment as a Director 
is not disquali/f_ied for appointment under 
Section 164 of the Companies Act, 2013.d. The NRC shall consider the following 
attributes / criteria, whilst recommending to 
the Board the candidature for appointment 
as Director.
   i.  Quali/f_ications, expertise and 
experience of the Directors in their 
respective /f_ields;
   ii.  Personal, Professional or business 
standing; and
   iii. Diversity of the Board
e.  In case of re-appointment of Non-Executive 
Independent Directors, the Board shall 
take into consideration the performance 
evaluation of the Directors and their 
engagement levels.
f. In considering the appointment or 
reappointment of a Non-Executive Director 
with af/f_iliations to other companies in 
the same industry, the NRC shall assess 
any con/f_licts of interest and satisfy itself 
that these do not impair the Director’s 
independence or judgement.
 2. Criteria for selection of Executive Directors
   For the purpose of selection of the Executive 
Directors, the NRC shall identify persons of 
integrity who possess relevant expertise, 
experience and leadership qualities required for 
the position and shall take into consideration 
recommendations, if any, received from any 
member of the Board. 
   The NRC, taking into account the results of the 
performance evaluation as well as the feedback of 
the Board, including Non-Executive Independent 
Directors, continuously reviews the Management 
pipeline to ensure that there are robust plans 
for succession for both planned and unplanned 
situations. Such plans are reviewed on an annual 
basis, also taking into account the feedback 
from stakeholders, considering both internal and 
external candidates.

 3. Remuneration Policy
   The main aim of the Remuneration Policy (the 
“Policy”), which can be accessed at the weblink  
https://www.apollohospitals.com/sites/default/
/f_iles/2025-08/remuneration-_policy_executive_
directors.pdf, is to determine the pay for its 
Executive Directors and senior management 
personnel competitively based on market levels, 
at a suf/f_icient level to attract and retain talent, and 
the need to ensure that they are motivated to 
perform in the best interests of all stakeholders, 
including shareholders. Variable pay, based on 
meeting pre-determined corporate objectives, 
is an important component of the remuneration 
package offered to Executive Directors.
   The NRC, comprised solely of Independent 
Directors, receives independent advice from 
a compensation and bene/f_it consultant /f_irm, 
while reviewing the Executive Directors’ and 
senior management remuneration, including the 
Company’s overall pay positioning against the 
NIFTY 50, as well as a select group of market 
peers in the healthcare and broader services 
sectors, taking into account the Company’s 
scale and complexity, its organizational structure 
and the responsibilities associated with each 
executive role. 
   In determining the Policy, the NRC also takes 
into account the views of shareholders as well 
as third-party service providers, such as proxy 
advisors and ESG Ratings /f_irms. In addition, it 
takes into account internal factors, including 
remuneration trends and developments across 
the wider Apollo Group, to ensure fairness and 
consistency in its approach.
   As part of the Company’s engagement 
efforts with its stakeholders, views on Apollo Hospitals’ executive remuneration practices and 
disclosures are also solicited to ensure that they 
remain in line with market expectations. To this 
end, several positive steps were taken over the 
years to strengthen the Policy and disclosure 
regarding the application of the Policy, such as 
increasing the transparency surrounding the 
annual bonuses, adopting malus and clawback 
provisions, instituting a monetary cap on the 
commission payable to the Executive Chairman, 
and introducing a voluntary cap on total executive 
remuneration.
   During the period under review, Apollo Hospitals 
has:
  -  Increased the base salaries of the 
Executive Directors, excluding the 
Executive Chairman, by 10%, broadly 
in line with in/f_lationary trends and peer 
increase trends. For the coming year, the 
Company proposes a further increase of 
6% for Executive Directors, excluding the 
Executive Chairman, whose salary will 
remain unchanged to take into account 
in/f_lation, market movements in salaries and 
increase provided to the wider employee 
base.
  -   Awarded annual bonuses equal to 50% 
of the maximum opportunity for the 
Executive Chairman and 71% to 73% for 
the other Executive Directors, indicative of 
a stretching target setting framework.
  -  Awarded the Executive Chairman a 
commission of ` 75 million, re/f_lecting the 
NRC’s assessment of the Company’s 
/f_inancial and strategic performance and his 
individual contribution during the year.
  -  Transparently disclosed and limited 
bene/f_its provided to Executive Directors to 
Director’s and Of/f_icer’s Liability Insurance 
Policy, medical insurance, a car and driver 
for the performance of of/f_icial duties and 
other bene/f_its expressly provided under the 
Remuneration Policy.

 Key Changes to the Framework
In response to intensifying industry competition, 
particularly from private equity-backed entities, the 
NRC prioritised increasing the “at-risk” portion of 
pay for the Executive Directors in the prior year. This 
change was strongly endorsed by shareholders and 
proxy advisors through the Executive Director re-
elections at the 2025 Annual General Meeting, with 
FY2025-2026 the /f_irst year in which the increased 
opportunity applied.
 Annual Bonus Framework
As mentioned above, all Executive Director are eligible 
to receive a performance-based Annual Bonus of up 
to 100% of their base salary, with metrics aligned with 
the Company’s strategy. The Executive Directors, 
other than the Executive Chairman, are assessed 
against a combination of shared and differentiated 
performance areas. The shared, group-level metrics 
ensure alignment on common Company-wide 
objectives, while the differentiated Key Result Areas 
(“KRAs”) provide suf/f_icient focus on each Director’s 
speci/f_ic scope and responsibilities. The Executive 
Chairman, by contrast, is assessed against a single 
standalone metric, re/f_lecting his role in steering group 
performance. Speci/f_ically:
For the Executive Chairman, 100% of the annual bonus 
is linked to achievement of consolidated EBITDA (i.e. 
consolidated operating pro/f_its) targets.
For the other Executive Directors, 60% of the annual 
bonus is linked to shared, group-level /f_inancial 
and sustainability-linked performance metrics — 
comprising Revenue, EBITDA, Quality and Clinical 
Excellence, Net Promoter Score / patient satisfaction, 
and ESG measures (energy ef/f_iciency and gender 
parity) — ensuring collective accountability for 
Company-wide outcomes. The remaining 40% is 
assessed against individual KRAs, set annually by the 
NRC and aligned to each Director’s speci/f_ic remit:
Smt. Preetha Reddy, Executive Vice Chairperson: 
re/f_lecting her leadership of the hospital business, her 
KRAs cover the attraction and retention of doctors, 
clinical program development and outcomes, key 
hospital expansion projects, and growth in oncology 
and international patient revenue.
Smt. Suneeta Reddy, Managing Director: re/f_lecting 
her leadership of enterprise strategy and /f_inancial 
management, her KRAs cover capital allocation, 
center-of-excellence performance and market-share 
growth, and strategy implementation, new investments 
and sustainability.Smt. Sangita Reddy, Joint Managing Director: 
re/f_lecting her leadership of retail and integrated 
healthcare and of digital transformation, her KRAs cover 
retail healthcare revenue and EBITDA, technology and 
innovation, human capital management, and IT/digital 
strategy and policy advocacy.

6. OTHER DISCLOSURES 
 a. Related Party Transactions
 
  The Company appointed Price Waterhouse & Co 
LLP , India (“PWC”) to undertake a detailed review 
of all its key related party transactions such as 
purchase of pharmaceutical products, supply of 
pharmaceutical products and receipt of various 
services such as Food & Beverage services, 
manpower supply services, housekeeping 
services, etc. PWC relied on data provided by 
Apollo Hospitals Enterprises Limited (“AHEL”). 
The scope was limited to a review from an arm’s 
length price perspective.
   The transactions were undertaken in conjunction 
with the related party transaction policy approved 
by the Board and the results of the same were 
presented for analysis by PWC. PWC undertook 
a comparison of AHEL’s data with comparable 
price and observed that transactions are at arm’s 
length.
   Further, PWC also veri/f_ied on a sample basis, 
the below arrangements of purchase of 
pharmaceutical products from the network 
suppliers:
  - Provision of incremental discounts to AHEL;
  -  Scheme bene/f_its and price reductions 
offered by manufacturers are passed on to 
AHEL;
  -  Delivery on priority basis to AHEL thereby 
reducing its inventory holding cost;
  -  Logistic support – Special infrastructure 
backed delivery centres for AHEL and;
  -  Streamlined buying structure and integration 
of computer systems between AHEL and 
network suppliers.
   The details of transactions are disclosed in the 
notes forming part of the Accounts as required 
under Indian Accounting Standard (IND AS) 
24 noti/f_ied by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. Corporate Governance Report (Contd.)

SEBI has made it mandatory for listed 
companies to issue securities in demat 
mode only while processing any investor 
service requests viz. issue of duplicate 
share certi/f_icates, exchange/sub-division/ 
splitting/consolidation of securities, 
transmission/ transposition of securities

2026 SEBI has done away with requirement 
of issuance of Letter of Con/f_irmation (LOC) 
effective April 2, 2026 and to effect direct 
credit of securities in dematerialization 
account of the investor.  Any LOC issued 
before April 2, 2026, may be submitted by 
the shareholders to DP for demat within 120 
days from the date of issuance of LOC.
    Members holding shares in physical form 
are requested to consider converting their 
holdings to dematerialized form.

Annual Report 2025-26 134  4) Unclaimed Dividend / Shares
    Pursuant to Sections 124 and 125 of the Act read with the Investor Education and Protection Fund Authority 
(Accounting, Audit, Transfer and Refund) Rules, 2016 (IEPF Rules), dividends, if not claimed for a consecutive 
period of 7 years from the date of transfer to Unpaid Dividend Account of the Company, are liable to be 
transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (‘IEPF’).
    Further, shares in respect of such dividends which have not been claimed for a period of 7 consecutive 
years are also liable to be transferred to the demat account of the IEPF Authority. The said requirement does 
not apply to shares in respect of which there is a speci/f_ic order of a Court, Tribunal or Statutory Authority, 
restraining any transfer of the shares. 
    In the interest of the shareholders, the Company sends periodical reminders to the shareholders to claim their 
dividends in order to avoid transfer of dividends/shares to the IEPF Authority. Notices in this regard are also 
published in the newspapers. 
    In light of the aforesaid provisions, the Company has during the year, transferred to IEPF the unclaimed 
dividends, outstanding for 7 consecutive years, of the Company. Further, shares of the Company, in respect 
of which dividend has not been claimed for 7 consecutive years or more, have also been transferred to the 
demat account of the IEPF Authority.

Apollo Hospitals Enterprise Limited 151Business Review1.1  India’s GDP Performance and Outlook 
  India continues to remain one of the fastest-growing major economies globally, 
supported by resilient domestic demand, government-led infrastructure spending 
and improving investment activity. Following a contraction in FY21, the economy 
has demonstrated strong recovery and sustained growth momentum. 
  Real GDP growth stood at 9.2% in FY24, moderated to 6.5% in FY25 and 
recovered to 7.7% in FY26, re/f_lecting resilient domestic demand in the backdrop 
of a challenging global environment. 
Growth during FY26 was supported by healthy private consumption, sustained public capital expenditure, improving services 
activity and stable macroeconomic fundamentals. The country also bene/f_ited from a resilient banking system, increasing 
formalisation of the economy and continued investments across infrastructure and manufacturing sectors. 
Global economic growth remained moderate during FY26 amid geopolitical tensions, trade-related disruptions and uneven 
recovery across major economies. Looking ahead, the global environment continues to present uncertainties, particularly 
around trade /f_lows, commodity prices and geopolitical developments.
For India, growth is expected to remain robust with strong domestic demand, rising urbanisation, favourable demographics 
and increasing investments across key sectors of the economy. However, global trade disruptions, commodity price volatility, 
geopolitical developments and /f_luctuations in capital /f_lows may continue to in/f_luence the near-term economic outlook. Despite 
these uncertainties, India remains well positioned to sustain its growth momentum supported by its large domestic market, 
improving infrastructure and ongoing economic reforms.

1.3. India’s urbanisation expected to increase steadily 
  While India’s urbanisation levels remain lower than many developed economies, the country continues to witness steady 
migration towards urban centres. This ongoing urbanisation trend is expected to support demand for infrastructure and 
organised services across sectors. It is projected that 40% of India’s population will live in urban areas by the Year 2030.
1.4.  Rising incomes and consumption
  India’s per capita income increased to ` 98,374 in /f_iscal 2023, a CAGR of 4.1%, growing with increased GDP activity and 
rising job opportunities. Although India’s per capita income remains below that of developed economies, rising income 
levels and expanding middle-class consumption continue to improve affordability and support greater spending.India surpassed China to become 
the world’s populous country in 
2023. India’s population is estimated 
to touch 1.5 billion by 2030.  
Source: Crisil1.2  India emerges as the world’s most populous country 
  India has emerged as the world’s most populous country, accounting 
for approximately one-sixth of the global population. Compared to many 
developed economies facing ageing populations and slower workforce 
growth, India’s favourable demographic pro/f_ile and large working-age 
population continue to support long-term economic activity.
1.5.   Healthcare under-penetration and rising affordability support long-term growth
  Healthcare expenditure in India remains lower than many developed 
and emerging economies, indicating signi/f_icant headroom for growth as 
affordability, awareness and insurance penetration improve. In contrast, 
developed nations such as United States, Germany, France, Japan and 
the United Kingdom allocate higher share of their GDP to healthcare 
compared to developing countries like India, Vietnam and Indonesia.
  Compared to many developed markets with stronger public healthcare 
systems, private healthcare providers play a signi/f_icant role in India’s 
healthcare delivery ecosystem. The general expenditure on health as a 
% of Current Healthcare Expenditure was skewed towards Private Health 
expenditure at 67%. Capacity constraints in the public healthcare system, coupled with increasing demand for quality 
healthcare services, are expected to support long-term opportunities for organised healthcare providers.
1.6.  Healthcare infrastructure and talent
  India continues to face structural gaps in healthcare infrastructure and talent availability, including lower hospital bed 
and healthcare professional availability per capita compared to several global benchmarks. India had approximately 7.4 
physicians and 18 nurses per 10,000 population at the close of 2021. These gaps remain more pronounced across 
non-metro and underserved regions, highlighting the need for continued investment in healthcare infrastructure, talent 
development and capacity creation.

lifestyle-related ailments like hypertension, diabetes, etc is expected to sustain demand for healthcare services over the 
long term.
2.3.3.  Widening gaps in access and consumption  remains uneven across regions in India. Variations in infrastructure 
availability, particularly between urban and rural areas, continue to in/f_luence healthcare consumption patterns. 
Government initiatives aimed at improving affordability and access have strengthened the healthcare ecosystem. 
Government schemes such as Ayushman Bharat – Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) continue to improve 
healthcare access and support treatment affordability. However, infrastructure and distribution gaps persist across 
certain regions in India, creating opportunities for organised healthcare providers to expand their presence. 
2.3.4.  India’s disease proﬁle has undergone a structural shift, with Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs) accounting for a 
gr
owing share of the overall disease burden. Lifestyle-related risk factors such as unhealthy diets, sedentary lifestyles, 
hypertension, diabetes and obesity continue to contribute to rising incidence 
of cardiovascular diseases, cancer and metabolic disorders.

1.  Clinical Excellence and Speciality Focus:
 Apollo Hospitals continues to focus on delivering high-quality clinical outcomes across specialities, supported by 
experienced medical pr
ofessionals, advanced treatment capabilities and robust clinical protocols. The Group continues to 
strengthen its presence across high-acuity specialities such as cardiac care, oncology, neurosciences, gastroenterology 
and orthopaedics, supported by continued investments in advanced clinical capabilities and complex care programmes.
 Apollo Hospitals encourages all of its medical professionals and other employees to participate in ongoing medical 
education and skill development initiatives. To enhance patient outcomes, the group ensures that its professionals and 
staff remain up to date on the latest medical techniques and procedures.
 Eight hospitals in the group have received accreditation from the Joint Commission International, USA, in recognition 
of adherence to international healthcare quality standards for patient care and hospital management. JCI is the world’s 
premier accreditation body for patient safety and quality healthcare. Hospitals at Chennai, Bengaluru, New Delhi, 
Hyderabad, Kolkata, Ahmedabad, and Navi Mumbai are also accredited by both JCI and NABH. The total number of 
‘NABH’ accredited hospitals in the Group now stands at 33.

2.  Driving Operating Efficiency
 The core of Apollo Hospitals’ growth strategy is to maximise operating ef/f_iciency and pro/f_itability across the network. 
Gr
eater integration, improved supply chain management, and human resource development are the three essentials 
for increasing ef/f_iciencies. The goal is to reduce the cost of expensive drugs and medical consumables such as 
stents, implants, and other surgical materials by standardising across the network, optimising procurement costs, 
consolidating suppliers, and optimising use of medical consumables by establishing guidelines for medical procedures. 
These measures are critical for driving margin expansion, particularly in the context of rising input costs and regulatory  
price caps.
 Apollo Hospitals constantly endeavours to reduce the Average Length of Stay (ALOS) in its hospitals. Today, new 
advancements in medical technology, such as the introduction of minimally invasive and robot-assisted surgeries, have 
signi/f_icantly reduced surgical trauma and patient recovery time. These innovations not only enhance clinical differentiation 
but also contribute to higher ARPP (Average Revenue Per Patient) by enabling more complex, higher-value procedures.
3.  Technology and Innovation:
 Apollo Hospitals continues to strengthen its commitment to clinical excellence through the adoption of cutting-edge 
technologies and advanced medical pr
otocols. These advancements aim to elevate the standard of patient care and 
improve clinical outcomes across its network.
 Apollo has been at the forefront of medical innovation, having introduced several pioneering technologies in India—
including the country’s /f_irst MRI, CT, and PET CT systems; Asia’s most advanced Cyber Knife; and Proton Therapy for 
cancer treatment. 
 Apollo Hospitals continues to leverage technology to improve operational ef/f_iciency and expand healthcare access. 
Initiatives such as Apollo 24|7, digital health platforms, data analytics and advanced medical technologies continue to 
support integrated and personalised healthcare delivery.
4.  Medical Tourism:
 Assured Pricing Plans were introduced to address the disparity between the cost and pricing of surgical procedures, 
focusing on the intrinsic value of the deliver
ed service. These plans cover a wide range of surgical procedures and are 
designed to enhance transparency and predictability in healthcare costs. 
 This approach not only improves accessibility but also supports Apollo Hospitals in targeting and serving the growing 
Medical Value Travel (MVT) market. MVT has become a signi/f_icant focus area, as India’s competitive healthcare costs 
and advanced medical services attract international patients. 
 By aligning Assured Pricing Plans with MVT initiatives, Apollo Hospitals aims to strengthen its value proposition for 
international patients by offering both price assurance and access to high-quality clinical outcomes.
5.  Capacity Expansion and deepening presence in key markets:
 Apollo Hospitals maintains a signi/f_icant presence in major cities and urban centres, where there is sustained demand for 
high-quality tertiary car
e services such as transplants, robotics. 
 Presently, Apollo Hospitals has established hospitals in Tier II and Tier III cities, with ample room for growth given the 
existing capacity and operational beds. 
 During FY26, Apollo Hospitals commissioned the initial phase of beds across its new hospitals in Pune, Narendrapur 
(Kolkata), Hyderabad, and Delhi, with 185 beds becoming operational during the year. The Company continues to 
expand its network through hospital asset acquisitions, green/f_ield and brown/f_ield expansions across key markets 
including Gurgaon, Bengaluru, Mysuru, Mumbai, Chennai, Lucknow, Varanasi and Hyderabad.
6.  Service Excellence and Patient Centricity:
 Apollo Hospitals continues to strengthen patient-centred care through a combination of compassion, service excellence, 
post-discharge support, and digital innovation. Management Discussion & Analysis (Contd.)

 During FY 2025-26, the BEKIND initiative was expanded across the network, with over 24,000 employees trained in

such as Net Promoter Score (NPS). 
 Creating Tender Loving Care (TLC) moments and sharing kindness stories provides a platform for enhancing the

3.2.  Diagnostics and Retail Health
3.2.1 Overview
  Apollo Health & Lifestyle Limited (AHLL) focuses on bringing healthcare closer to communities through a network 
of clinics, diagnostic centres and specialised care facilities. Built on a scalable hub-and-spoke model, AHLL enhances 
healthcare accessibility by delivering integrated, patient-centric outpatient and preventive care across a wide spectrum 
of patient needs.
  AHLL operates a multi-brand portfolio across diagnostics, primary care and specialised healthcare services. The 
Company runs the largest chain of standardised primary healthcare models Apollo Clinics – multi-specialty clinics in 
India and Middle East, Apollo Sugar – Diabetes management clinics, Apollo Cradle – for Women & Children, Apollo 
Spectra – for planned surgery and Apollo Diagnostics – Diagnostic tests.
  These diverse offerings aim to position AHLL as the preferred family healthcare partner, blending comprehensive 
capabilities with local care. This scalable and replicable model has the potential to rede/f_ine integrated healthcare 
accessibility in the country

3.3. Digital Health and Pharmacy Distribution
  Apollo HealthCo represents Apollo Hospitals’ integrated omni-channel platform, combining pharmacy distribution, digital 
health and consumer healthcare services. The platform plays a critical role in extending the Group’s reach beyond 
hospitals by enabling seamless access to medicines, healthcare products and services across both physical and digital 
channels.
  The business comprises a large, organised pharmacy network, a nationwide pharmaceutical distribution platform 
and the Apollo 24|7 digital health interface. This integrated model enables stronger customer engagement, improved 
accessibility and continuity of care across the patient lifecycle, while also driving operational ef/f_iciencies through scale 
and supply chain integration.
  Apollo HealthCo bene/f_its from its strong sourcing capabilities and extensive distribution network, which support cost 
ef/f_iciencies and improved product availability. The growing contribution of private label and generic products remains an 
important focus area, supporting margin improvement and enhancing the overall value proposition for customers.
  During FY26, the Company progressed its strategic initiative through a 
Composite Scheme of Arrangement involving the demerger of its omni-
channel pharmacy distribution, Apollo 24|7 digital platform and remote 
telehealth businesses into Apollo Healthtech Limited, followed by the 
amalgamation of Apollo HealthCo Limited and Keimed Private Limited 
into the resultant entity. The proposed restructuring is intended to enable 
sharper strategic focus, dedicated management oversight, improved 
capital allocation and better value discovery through two distinct equity 
stories.
  Apollo HealthCo plays a pivotal role in strengthening Apollo Hospitals’ integrated healthcare ecosystem by bridging 
physical and digital healthcare delivery. The platform enhances patient engagement, supports cross-utilization across 
the Apollo ecosystem and enables a more connected, consumer-centric healthcare experience.

5.  RISKS AND CONCERNS 
  Apollo Hospitals operates at a signi/f_icantly larger scale today, with an expanded and diversi/f_ied business footprint, which 
exposes the organisation to a br
oader spectrum of risks and uncertainties compared to the past. These internal and 
external factors may in/f_luence the achievement of its strategic, operational and /f_inancial objectives.
  The operating environment continues to be characterised by increasing competition and evolving market dynamics. In 
the normal course of business, the Company is exposed to a range of risks, which are  an inherent part of any growth-
oriented enterprise and are often accompanied by opportunities for value creation.
  The Company also remains exposed to external risks arising from geopolitical developments, macroeconomic 
uncertainties and foreign exchange /f_luctuations. Recent geopolitical developments, have led to some moderation in 
international patient in/f_lows and medical value travel in the near term. While the long-term outlook remains stable, 
any prolonged disruption may temporarily impact international patient in/f_lows and medical value travel. In addition, 
movements in the Indian Rupee against major currencies, particularly the US Dollar, may in/f_luence the cost of imported 
medical equipment, consumables and certain technology-related expenditures, thereby impacting operating costs. The 
Company continues to actively monitor these external risks and implement appropriate mitigation measures.
  Apollo Hospitals recognizes that continuous identi/f_ication and assessment 
of business sustainability risks, along with their integration into the 
existing risk management framework, are critical to long-term success. 
The Group has instituted processes that strengthen risk awareness and 
promote a robust, organisation-wide risk management culture. 
  Under the oversight of the Board of Directors, senior management across 
business units actively monitors and manages risks. While risks cannot 
be entirely eliminated, appropriate mitigation strategies are implemented 
for areas with signi/f_icant exposure. The risk management framework is 
designed to ensure that risks remain within acceptable and manageable thresholds.
5.1  Internal Controls
  Apollo Hospitals is committed to maintaining a robust internal control 
environment across its operations. The Company’s integrated internal 
control framework supports the safeguarding of assets, accuracy of 
/f_inancial and management reporting, and compliance with applicable 
laws, regulations and internal policies. 
  While no internal control system can provide absolute assurance against
